results.blind_working: v_d = eτE/m with E = V/L. New E = 2V/(L/2) = 4E, so v_d becomes 4 times.

A is true: the electric field is set up throughout the wire almost instantly, so electrons everywhere start drifting at once. R is true: thermal speeds are about 10^5 m/s. But random thermal motion does not explain the immediate glow.
I is correct: μ = eτ/m, unit m^2V^-1s^-1. II is wrong: since μ = eτ/m, a fall in τ also lowers the mobility.
At constant volume R ∝ L². Tripling the length gives R' = 9 × 5 = 45 Ω.
Halving the diameter makes A' = A/4. At constant volume R ∝ 1/A², so R' = 16 × 4 = 64 Ω.
A: double length gives 4R (IV). B: half radius makes area 1/4, giving 16R (III). C: each of 4 parts is R/4 (II). D: area 1/3 gives 9R (I).
A is false because resistivity is a material property and does not change on stretching. B, C and D are true. E is false because the SI unit of conductance is the siemens, not ohm-metre.
Ohm's law holds for a metal wire only at constant temperature. In that case V ∝ I, so the graph is a straight line through the origin. A diode, a filament lamp and a voltameter are all non-linear.
With V on the y-axis and I on the x-axis, R equals the slope. So R = tan60° = √3 Ω.
The slope of an I-V graph is 1/R. This gives R1 = 1/0.5 = 2 Ω and R2 = 1/0.25 = 4 Ω. A metal's resistance rises with temperature, so T2 > T1, and R at T2 is 4 Ω.
Passing through the origin does not make a device ohmic. A filament bulb's resistance rises as it heats, so its V-I graph is non-linear and it is non-ohmic. Hence A is false and R is true.
For a non-ohmic device, dV/dI is generally not equal to V/I, so I is false. GaAs has a negative-resistance region where the same current occurs at more than one voltage, so II is true.

A true: in series P = I^2R and the lower-wattage bulb has larger R. B false: in parallel P = V^2/R, so the smaller R dissipates more. C true: higher V means lower I, so less I^2R loss. D false: P ∝ V^2, so power becomes 1/4 of rated. E true: R = V^2/P. Correct set is A, C, E.
Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity. Resistivity is in Ω m, so conductivity is in Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ = S m⁻¹.
ρ = m/(ne²τ), so ρA/ρB = (nB τB)/(nA τA) = 1/(2 × 1/4) = 2.
Resistivity is a material property that depends on material and temperature, not on dimensions. Stretching changes R but not ρ, so A is true and R is false.
I: ρ = m/(ne²τ), so larger τ gives smaller ρ; I is false. II: manganin is chosen for its very low temperature coefficient, and its resistivity is higher than copper's; II is false.
In series nR = 100 and in parallel R/n = 4. Multiplying gives R² = 400, so R = 20 Ω and n = 5.
3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel give 2 Ω, so the total is 6 Ω and I = 18/6 = 3 A. The voltage across the parallel pair is 3 × 2 = 6 V, so the current through 6 Ω is 6/6 = 1 A.
A: series gives 18 Ω. B: parallel gives 2 Ω. C: 3 + 6 = 9 Ω. D: 12 Ω parallel with 6 Ω gives 4 Ω. So A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II.

A is true. B is true. C is false: in parallel, current divides inversely with resistance. D is true: equal potentials mean no current. E is false: R_series ≥ n² R_parallel, with equality for equal resistors, so it is never less. Correct set is A, B, D.
Pure metals (Cu, Al) have a positive coefficient, and manganin's is nearly zero. Germanium, a semiconductor, has a negative coefficient.
A common (NTC) thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature rises, so A is false. R correctly states that semiconductor resistivity falls with temperature, so R is true.
Take R1 = R0(1 + a*dT) and R2 = R0(1 - a*dT). In parallel, conductance = 2/[R0(1 - a^2 dT^2)], which depends on temperature, so I is incorrect. In series, R1 + R2 = 2R0 exactly, so II is correct.
While charging, V = ε + Ir = 12 + 5(0.2) = 13 V
Maximum power occurs at R = r, so Pmax = ε²/4r = 36/6 = 6 W

A is correct: emf is work per unit charge by the non-electrostatic force, in volts. B is correct: V = ε - Ir. C is false: efficiency is only 50% at maximum power. D is correct: larger electrode area and higher temperature lower r. E is false: r increases as the cell ages.
Net emf = 4 × 1.5 = 6 V. Total internal resistance = 4 × 0.5 = 2 Ω. I = 6/(4+2) = 1.0 A.
With two cells reversed, net emf = (4−2) × 2 = 4 V. Internal resistance stays 6 × 0.5 = 3 Ω. I = 4/(7+3) = 0.4 A.

Series current = nε/(R+nr) ≈ nε/R. Parallel current = ε/(R + r/n) ≈ ε/R. So series gives the larger current and A is true. R correctly states why: the emf adds to nε in series while the resistance stays nearly R, but the emf remains ε in parallel.
I: circulating current = (3−1)/(1+1) = 1 A, so I is correct. II: net emf = (7−3) × 1.5 = 6 V, but internal resistance = 10 × 0.2 = 2 Ω, not 0.8 Ω, so II is incorrect.
By Kirchhoff's junction rule, current in equals current out. In: 5 + 3 = 8 A. Out so far: 2 A. So the fourth wire carries 8 − 2 = 6 A leaving the junction.

Walk from A to B. The 3 Ω resistor gives a drop of 2 × 3 = 6 V. The cell, crossed from − to +, gives a rise of 5 V. The 2 Ω resistor gives a drop of 2 × 2 = 4 V. So V_A − 6 + 5 − 4 = V_B, giving V_A − V_B = 5 V.
Take N as 0 V and let P be at V. Node equation at P: (12 − V)/2 + (6 − V)/2 = V/2, so 18 − 2V = V and V = 6 V. Current through the 6 V cell = (6 − 6)/2 = 0.

The junction rule expresses conservation of charge (A-III). The loop rule expresses conservation of energy (B-II). Crossing a resistor along the assumed current gives a change of −IR (C-I). A negative current means the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction (D-IV).

A is true: independent loops = b − n + 1 = 6 − 4 + 1 = 3. B is true: the loop rule holds because the electrostatic field is conservative. C is false: the laws also apply to quasi-static AC circuits. D is false: potential difference is path-independent. E is true: this describes the node method. Correct set is A, B and E.
Rearranging P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 6×8/4 = 12 Ω.
AB/BC = 2/4 and AD/DC = 3/6, so the bridge is balanced and the 10 Ω resistor carries no current. Path ABC = 6 Ω and path ADC = 9 Ω in parallel give 54/15 = 3.6 Ω.

Doubling both P and S changes the condition to 2P/Q vs R/(2S), which is no longer equal, so the balance is disturbed. Changing the emf, swapping the cell and galvanometer, or changing the galvanometer resistance keeps the balance.

A is true: the balance condition involves only the four arm resistances. R is true: sensitivity is greatest when the resistances are of the same order. R is about sensitivity, so it does not explain A.

I: 10/20 = 15/30, so the bridge is balanced and no current flows in the galvanometer arm. Shorting the 5 Ω resistor therefore changes nothing, so I is true. II: after the swap, 20/10 ≠ 15/30, so the bridge is unbalanced and II is false.
Balance condition: R/S = l/(100 - l). So 6/S = 40/60, giving S = 9 Ω.
Initially R/S = 25/75, so S = 3R. Shunting S by an equal resistance makes it S/2 = 1.5R. Then R/(1.5R) = l/(100 - l), so l/(100 - l) = 2/3 and l = 40 cm.

The null point depends only on the ratio R/S. Changing the cell emf, adding series resistance or changing galvanometer sensitivity leaves R/S unchanged. Heating S changes its resistance, so the null point shifts.

A: the wire is manganin or constantan (IV). B: interchanging R and S moves the null point from l to 100 - l (I). C: heating raises S, so l decreases and the point shifts towards R (II). D: shunting lowers S, so l increases and the point shifts towards S (III).

A is true: accuracy is best near 50 cm. B is false: the wire is manganin or constantan, not copper. C is true: this is the end-correction form. D is false: the jockey should be tapped, not slid while pressed. E is true: interchanging R and S and averaging reduces error. So A, C and E.
